kept.title: A refused WebSocket upgrade can crash the whole console (its socket has no error handler)
kept.attacker: anyone on the internet
kept.attack: Send any /console/api request with `Connection: Upgrade` and `Upgrade: websocket`, drop the connection, and repeat (it is a race). Node removes its own error listener before the upgrade event; editorUpgrade answers with socket.end() and adds none. When Tailscale has closed its side first, the write fails, the socket emits an unhandled error and the process exits (only unhandledRejection is caught). systemd restarts it 3 seconds later with jobs, claims, buttons and sign-in codes lost. A refused upgrade sent with a body also leaves its socket open for good.
kept.wiring: service/src/25-backup-and-start.mjs:39 (every upgrade on the Funnel socket → editorUpgrade) → 21-editor.mjs:76 (deny = socket.end) → :80, :81, :83, :104 (every refusal) → no socket.on('error') until :94 → 25-backup-and-start.mjs:80 (only unhandledRejection is handled) → deploy/host-on-portal.sh:192-195 (Restart=always, RestartSec=3, MemoryMax=512M); docs/architecture.md:247 (restarts forget)
kept.fix: In editorUpgrade, first line: socket.on('error', () => {}); make deny end the socket and then destroy it: socket.end(text, () => socket.destroy()). Do the same in the two one-line upgrade handlers at 25-backup-and-start.mjs:40-41. Beside line 80, also log (not exit) on uncaughtException. Add a test that resets a refused upgrade.
kept.verifierNote: Every step holds in code: Node removes its socket error listener before 'upgrade' (checked in Node's source), deny() at 21-editor.mjs:76 adds none, and only unhandledRejection is caught. Tailscale forwards Upgrade and closes the backend socket when the visitor leaves. A timing race, not run live. The open-socket claim needs body bytes arriving after the headers.

kept.attacker: anyone on the internet

The table then holds 300 waiting codes, so line 194 answers the owner's new terminal or phone with 429 for as long as it is kept full. The same pool, sending 30 /auth/signin/begin calls each per 10 minutes, keeps the shared 3,000 budget used, so the owner's passkey sign-in gets 429 too. Devices already signed in, and Tailscale, keep working.

Tailscale sets X-Forwarded-For to the visitor's real address, so about 100 addresses are needed for passkey sign-in. The code path needs fewer: 10 addresses use up the 4,000 poll budget. Signed-in devices and Tailscale skip these limits.

kept.title: A request for /console/api// is never answered and logs a stack trace (the URL is parsed outside the try)
kept.attacker: anyone on the internet
kept.attack: GET /console/api// on port 8443. Tailscale strips the mount and passes the path `//`. `new URL('//', 'http://local')` throws at line 50, outside the try that starts at line 52 and before /health and requestGate. The handler's promise rejects, line 80 logs `Unhandled: TypeError: Invalid URL` with a stack, and no answer is ever sent: the request hangs until the sender leaves. A loop of these floods the journal and holds sockets open with no timeout.
kept.wiring: service/src/24-handler.mjs:50 (new URL, before the try at :52) → 25-backup-and-start.mjs:37-38 (the handler's promise is not caught) → :80 (logged only, no response)
kept.fix: Move the URL parse (lines 50-51) inside the try, or catch it and answer 400. The door and local listeners share this handler, so one change covers all three.
kept.verifierNote: new URL('//', 'http://local') throws (run in Node) at 24-handler.mjs:50, before the try. Tailscale strips /console/api with StripPrefix and forwards '//' unchanged, with no response timeout. Only unhandledRejection logs it; no answer is sent. Sockets stay held only while the sender keeps its own connection open.

kept.title: A flood from about 100 addresses blocks every new sign-in from the internet
kept.attacker: anyone on the internet
kept.attack: They POST /auth/signin/begin (with X-Spark-Console: 1) 30 times from each of about 100 addresses every 10 minutes. Each address stays under its own cap, the shared count reaches 3000, and the owner's begin and sign-in get 429. Codes fall the same way: junk polls from 10 addresses fill the 4000 poll cap, which is counted before the code is looked up, and 100 addresses fill the 300-code table. Devices already signed in, and Tailscale, keep working.

Codes: 22-sessions.mjs:189 (10 / 600), :193-194 (300 waiting, 3 per address), :203 (400 / 4000, before the lookup at :206-208). public/app.js:2063-2072 and tools/console.mjs:114 retry a 429 poll silently until the code ends. Address: 24-handler.mjs:35.
kept.fix: Remove the overall cap from /auth/signin/begin and /auth/signin; keep the per-address one. Challenges are signed, not stored, and a passkey answer can't be guessed, so the cap protects nothing. In /auth/device/poll, look the code up first and count only unknown codes. Code starts stay limited: the passkey is the path that must always work.
kept.verifierNote: Holds. limited() checks the shared '*' count after the per-address one; begin and sign-in share signinHits (30/3000), so just over 100 addresses give the owner 429. Tailscale sets X-Forwarded-For to the real Funnel client, so nothing earlier stops it. Poll is counted before lookup. Sessions and tailnet keep working. If the cap goes, bound signinUsed.

kept.title: The editor proxy puts any web server on a Spark under the console's own origin (code-server's /proxy/<port>/)

A click from the console's page or another app is not cross-site, so the page loads in the console's origin. Its script calls the API with X-Spark-Console and opens Spark 2's editor WebSocket: a shell.

The editor unit's flags are not in this repo. Needs a program on a Spark plus one click, hence medium.

kept.title: The sign-in cookie is also sent to the public app on port 443 (known, still open)

Any page of the port-443 app (or markup injected into it) that loads https://<same host>/console/api/x makes the owner's signed-in browser send the token to that app's server. SameSite=Strict does not stop it: it is the same site. Whoever reads that server's requests or logs replays the token through Funnel from anywhere and is the owner for up to 180 days (session-1).

kept.fix: Owner only: point port 443's /console/api at nothing (the planned tailscale serve command), or move the public app to another hostname. In code, session-1's step-up limits what a leaked cookie is worth. Neither stops port 443 setting cookies (session-5).

Only the port-443 app's server receives it: an outside page can neither trigger it (SameSite=Strict) nor read it. So it needs that app taken over or its request logs read; then session-1 applies.

kept.title: GET requests skip the cross-site check: another site can make the owner's browser run unlimited probes on the Sparks
kept.attacker: a web page the owner visits

kept.attacker: a web page the owner visits

A shell needs a taken-over door, Chromium, and that check missing or widened.

kept.title: A signed-in browser session opens VS Code (a full shell on every Spark) with no passkey
kept.attacker: someone with a stolen session cookie

kept.title: About thirty large /v1 calls at once run the console out of its 512 MB and it is killed
kept.attacker: a program on one of the Sparks
kept.attack: A program on any Spark needs no key for /v1. It opens 30 calls at once, each an 8 MB JSON body (the bulk in a field engines ignore) asking for a long answer, so they stay open or queued. Each call keeps its parsed body (req.bodyPromise) and a second copy (payload) until it ends, about 16 MB. Nothing caps calls in flight. The unit's MemoryMax=512M kills the service; systemd restarts it with operations cut off and claims forgotten. Repeat. A look-only key does the same from the internet.
kept.wiring: 24-handler.mjs:44 (a Spark's address may reach /v1) -> 03-identity.mjs:159-165 (it is the owner) -> 24-handler.mjs:118 -> 15-routes.mjs:157 (8e6 limit) -> 23-http.mjs:8-9, :25 (parsed body kept on req.bodyPromise) -> 15-routes.mjs:181-197 or :85-100 (payload held until the reply ends; no time limit, no count) -> 25-backup-and-start.mjs:37 (no connection limit) -> deploy/host-on-portal.sh:192-195 (Restart=always, MemoryMax=512M)
kept.fix: Cap /v1 calls in flight (for example 8 in all and 3 per caller, 429 beyond), drop the kept copy once the payload is built (req.bodyPromise = null), and give each upstream call a time limit. Per-caller caps keep one caller from shutting the owner's own apps out.
kept.verifierNote: Holds, and is easier than stated: readBody keeps up to 8e6 characters per call (16 MB for non-Latin text), plus the parsed copy and payload. A sender that stalls before the last byte holds them for Node's 5-minute request timeout with no model involved. No cap on calls; MemoryMax=512M, Restart=always (host-on-portal.sh:192-195).

The brain is callable by its served name even if agents are routed elsewhere. The page and actions keep working. background:true on SGLang not verified.

kept.title: A WebSocket-style request that is then reset can stop the whole service: upgrade sockets have no error handler
kept.attacker: a program on one of the Sparks
kept.attack: A program on Spark 2 connects to 127.0.0.1:8810 and sends any request with Connection: Upgrade. The program resets the connection: an 'error' with no listener is an uncaught exception, and only unhandledRejection is caught, so the process exits and systemd restarts it. Repeat. kept.verifierNote: Node's source removes the socket's error listener before emitting 'upgrade'; all three handlers answer with socket.end and add none; only unhandledRejection is caught. A reset on 127.0.0.1:8810 ends the process. Through Tailscale, before sign-in, the 403 write gets EPIPE if tailscaled hangs up first (visitor aborts): plausible, not shown. If it works, this is high.

kept.title: For up to a minute after Tailscale or Spark 2 restarts, a program on a Spark is the owner over IPv6
kept.attacker: a program on one of the Sparks

The blocked list is rebuilt from one `tailscale status` answer and replaces the old one; an answer without peers (Tailscale just restarted) or a failed first answer (Spark Console started first, after a reboot) leaves the other Sparks' IPv4 addresses only. A Spark's IPv6 X-Forwarded-For then passes requestGate and viewerFor names the owner. Needs host-network code on a Spark and a restart it cannot trigger: medium, not high.

kept.attacker: anyone on the internet

kept.title: Large bodies at the model address can push the service past its memory limit
kept.attacker: a program on one of the Sparks
kept.attack: A program on any Spark (Tailscale vouches for it as the owner, and /v1 is open to it) opens about 40 connections to /console/api/v1/chat/completions and sends a JSON body of under 8 million characters on each, slowly. readBody keeps each one in memory while it arrives, and nothing limits how many arrive at once. kept.title: Whoever holds port 8810 first keeps Spark Console from starting

The ten places for unchecked asks are full and each stays a week. Every later ask from a real person is dropped, yet still answered 202, so neither they nor the owner learn of it. kept.verifierNote: undo_update is fleet:act with no inputs and no workflow, and returns no operation, so the hourly count skips it; undoUpdate runs the newest snapshot's restore.sh (files and unit, not state) and restarts. POST /rollback is not in needsPasskey. Limits: one build back only, refused while a job runs or agents are paused. Owner's stated choice (contract 8.7).

kept.title: A terminal's sign-in is a full owner session kept in a plain file, next to the look-only agent key

Passkey sign-in: the challenge is signed, single-use and lives 3 minutes (22-sessions.mjs:119-137); the origin must be the main address, so a page on port 443 or the short address is refused (22-passkey.mjs:16-18, service/passkey.mjs:97); domain hash, user-verified flag and signature are checked (passkey.mjs:124-137); a change-confirmation answer cannot be replayed as a sign-in (different challenge shape, 22-sessions.mjs:129 against 22-passkey.mjs:42).

Sign-in challenges: 16 random bytes plus an end time, signed with a key made at start-up, good for 3 minutes, used once, only in the exact spelling given out, and marked used before the answer is checked (22-sessions.mjs:119-137). A replayed answer, an altered challenge or one from before a restart is refused.

Confirm and register challenges: random, one use, 3 minutes, tied to the owner's login, the purpose and (for confirm) a hash of method, path and body (22-passkey.mjs:36-45, :91-96, :162-163). A sign-in answer can't be used as a confirmation or the other way round: different stores, different challenge shapes, and the type check (passkey.mjs:95).

The assertion check: the key and algorithm come from the stored passkey, never from the request; the signed domain hash must match the stored one; user present and user verified are both required; the signature covers the authenticator data and the hash of the exact client data bytes (passkey.mjs:124-137). Malformed input throws inside a try and becomes a 403 (22-sessions.mjs:177).

Registering a passkey: owner only; once a passkey exists it needs a passkey confirmation bound to the exact registration body; the first one is refused through Funnel and through the short address (24-handler.mjs:164, :189-196; 22-passkey.mjs:121, :154-165). CBOR reader: only reached after those gates, so its bytes come from the owner. It is bounded anyway: depth 8, arrays and maps of 1000 at most, every length checked against the buffer, no indefinite lengths, tags or floats, input at most 20,000 characters (passkey.mjs:9-12, :16-47).
Algorithms: only ES256 on P-256 with 32-byte coordinates, RS256 with exponent 65537 and a real modulus of 2048 bits or more, and Ed25519 (passkey.mjs:50-69, :117-119).

Device codes: the short code is only ever used by the owner's approve; collecting the session needs the 32-byte secret given to the device that started it, compared in constant time; approve needs the passkey bound to that code and is refused with no passkey; one collection; 10 minutes; never through the short address (22-sessions.mjs:196-215, :224-231; 22-passkey.mjs:127; 24-handler.mjs:76).
No lock-out from wrong answers: a failed passkey answer locks nothing, and a counter that goes backwards is reported, not refused (passkey.mjs:138-141; 22-passkey.mjs:32-35).

The address used for the limits can't be forged: Tailscale replaces X-Forwarded-For with the real sender (for Funnel, the public address), and an IPv6 /64 counts as one (24-handler.mjs:35; 03-identity.mjs:87-95). Checked in Tailscale's serve code.

Cross-site: the sign-in routes need the page's header and a matching origin (22-sessions.mjs:147-149); a browser can't send that header to another site without a preflight the service never answers. X-Forwarded-Host is the Host the browser sent, which a web page can't choose.

A Spark's own address can't use the sign-in routes or act as a person (24-handler.mjs:44); a session token is never accepted through the short address (22-sessions.mjs:53).

holdsUp: A client cannot supply or shadow Tailscale-User-Login, Tailscale-Funnel-Request or X-Forwarded-For through serve, on the main address or the short one. Tailscale deletes the incoming copies (underscore spellings too) and then sets its own, and runs Go's proxy in Rewrite mode, so a `Connection:` header naming them cannot strip what Tailscale adds (tailscale ipn/ipnlocal/serve.go: addTailscaleIdentityHeaders, addProxyForwardedHeaders). Relied on at 03-identity.mjs:158-159 and 24-handler.mjs:40, :64-65.

clientAddress taking the last X-Forwarded-For entry is right (24-handler.mjs:35): serve sets exactly one value, the sender's address, and Go removes any X-Forwarded-* the client sent before that. Through Funnel it is the visitor's public address as reported by Tailscale's ingress, so per-address limits cannot be dodged by sending a forged header.

Funnel traffic never gets a tailnet login: serve returns right after setting the Funnel header, before it looks the sender up; the service also ignores any login when that header is present (03-identity.mjs:158-159) and lets only public routes or a carried credential through (24-handler.mjs:40).

A container on Spark 2's Docker bridge (172.x), a loopback-sourced connection, or a tagged device gets no login from Tailscale (its lookup only matches a device's own tailnet addresses; tagged devices are skipped), so it is nobody and stops at the 401 (24-handler.mjs:99). This settles the 'not checked' note in docs/analysis-2026-11-11/01-gap-analysis-skeptics.json:409.

The /v1 exception for the Sparks cannot be stretched with path tricks: the gate (24-handler.mjs:44), the router (:104, :118) and sparkieApi (15-routes.mjs:156) all use one normalised pathname (24-handler.mjs:50-51), so /v1/../actions/x, %2e%2e, backslashes and //host/path are resolved before the check; a Spark's call never starts a model (15-routes.mjs:172-173).

A made-up `Authorization: Bearer x` gets a Funnel request past requestGate (22-sessions.mjs:51) but nothing before the 401 at 24-handler.mjs:99 reads a body or changes anything for it; tokens are 256 random bits, compared in constant time against hashes (22-sessions.mjs:58-59, 20-mcp.mjs:37-38).

The short address stays limited whatever headers arrive on its socket: no sign-in (24-handler.mjs:76), no sessions (22-sessions.mjs:53), no agent keys (24-handler.mjs:81), no editors or WebSockets (24-handler.mjs:59, 25-backup-and-start.mjs:41), no passkey confirmation (22-passkey.mjs:157). Floods cannot push out the owner's passkey challenge or grow memory without bound: sign-in challenges are signed and not stored (22-sessions.mjs:119-137), each limit map is capped at 2,000 addresses with an IPv6 /64 counted once (03-identity.mjs:87-104), device codes at 300 (22-sessions.mjs:194), confirm challenges at 150 (22-passkey.mjs:41).
